Your 3-day path to the HSBC technical round

This is a workbook, not a reading list. Each topic has a short lesson, exercises to try before you see the answer, and interview questions to say out loud. Everything is in Python, and every code solution on this page was run and tested.

Candidates who interviewed for HSBC technical roles in India report questions on core subjects (OS, DBMS, SQL, networks), coding a data structure such as a queue from scratch, and detailed discussion of their projects. The exact format and platform depend on your drive, so confirm those in your invite. The skills below are the same either way.

Coding and OOP, about 9 hours

  • MorningPython toolkit, stack and queue, hashmaps (Modules 1 to 3)
  • AfternoonArrays and strings, linked lists (Modules 4 and 5)

How to work through it

  1. Type every solution yourself in an editor or an online Python editor. Copy-pasting teaches you nothing.
  2. The 20-minute rule. Try each exercise for 20 minutes before opening the solution. If you are stuck, read only the approach, close it, and try again.
  3. Talk while you code. Explaining your thinking out loud is scored in a live interview, so practise it now.
  4. Short on time? Do the exercises marked Priority first.
  5. Tick Mark as done as you go. Progress is saved in this browser on this device.

Day 1Module 1, about 60 minutes

Python toolkit and warm-ups

Interviewers let you pick your language, and Python is a strong choice because the standard library does a lot of the work. The catch is that you must know what each operation costs, because "it works" is not enough. You have to say how fast it is.

Big-O in one minute

Big-O describes how the work grows as the input size n grows. You state it in every coding answer.

ComplexityNameTypical example
O(1)constantdictionary lookup, list index, push on a stack
O(log n)logarithmicbinary search (halving the range each step)
O(n)linearone loop over the input
O(n log n)linearithmicgood sorting algorithms
O(n²)quadratica loop inside a loop over the same input

How to say it in an interview

"This loops once over the array with O(1) dictionary lookups, so time is O(n). The dictionary can hold up to n items, so space is also O(n)." Always give both time and space.

What Python operations cost

Operationlistdict or setdeque
Add at the endO(1)O(1) averageO(1)
Remove from the endO(1)O(1) averageO(1)
Remove or insert at the frontO(n)not applicableO(1)
Check x in ...O(n)O(1) averageO(n)
Index a[i]O(1)lookup by key O(1)O(1) at the ends, O(n) in the middle
SortO(n log n)not applicablenot applicable

The toolkit

Read this block slowly and type it into a Python file. The comments show what each line returns.

from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque
import heapq

nums = [5, 3, 8, 3, 5, 5]

Counter(nums)                    # Counter({5: 3, 3: 2, 8: 1})
Counter(nums).most_common(1)     # [(5, 3)]

groups = defaultdict(list)       # a missing key becomes an empty list
groups["a"].append(1)

q = deque([1, 2, 3])
q.append(4)                      # add on the right, O(1)
q.popleft()                      # remove from the left, O(1)

heap = []
heapq.heappush(heap, 5)          # min-heap
heapq.heappush(heap, 2)
heapq.heappop(heap)              # 2, the smallest

words = ["pear", "fig", "apple"]
sorted(words, key=len)                       # ['fig', 'pear', 'apple']
sorted(words, key=lambda w: (-len(w), w))    # longest first, ties A-Z

for i, w in enumerate(words):    # index and value together
    pass

s = "hello"
s[::-1]                          # 'olleh'
s[1:3]                           # 'el'
nums[-1]                         # last element

Try it: Two most common words

Priority

Write top_two_words(text) that returns the two most common words as a list of (word, count) pairs, ignoring upper or lower case.

top_two_words("a b A c b a")   # [('a', 3), ('b', 2)]

Hint: split the text, then look at collections.Counter.

Show solution and explanation
from collections import Counter

def top_two_words(text):
    words = text.lower().split()
    return Counter(words).most_common(2)

lower() makes "A" and "a" count as the same word, split() breaks the text on whitespace, and Counter(...).most_common(2) returns the top two. Time is O(n) to count, plus a small sort of the distinct words. Space is O(n).

Edge cases to mention: empty text (returns an empty list), and punctuation like "hello," which would count separately unless you strip it.

Classic warm-ups

Campus interviews often start with easy classics to see if you can write clean code under pressure. You should be able to write these in under two minutes each.

Try it: Five classics from memory

Priority

Write these five functions without looking anything up:

  • reverse_string(s)
  • is_prime(n). Be ready to explain why you can stop at the square root.
  • fib(n), iterative. Then write it again with recursion and memoization.
  • fizzbuzz(n), returning a list of strings
  • count_vowels(s)
Show solution and explanation
def reverse_string(s):
    return s[::-1]

def is_prime(n):
    if n < 2:
        return False
    i = 2
    while i * i <= n:          # only test up to the square root
        if n % i == 0:
            return False
        i += 1
    return True

def fib(n):                    # iterative: O(n) time, O(1) space
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return a

def fizzbuzz(n):
    out = []
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        if i % 15 == 0:
            out.append("FizzBuzz")
        elif i % 3 == 0:
            out.append("Fizz")
        elif i % 5 == 0:
            out.append("Buzz")
        else:
            out.append(str(i))
    return out

def count_vowels(s):
    return sum(1 for ch in s.lower() if ch in "aeiou")

Why the square root? If n has a factor larger than its square root, it must also have a matching factor smaller than it. So if no factor turns up by √n, none exists. That makes it O(√n) instead of O(n).

Order matters in FizzBuzz. Test i % 15 first, because a multiple of 15 is also a multiple of 3 and 5.

The recursive Fibonacci with memoization (caching results so each value is computed once):

from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def fib_recursive(n):
    if n < 2:
        return n
    return fib_recursive(n - 1) + fib_recursive(n - 2)

Plain recursion without the cache recomputes the same values again and again, taking O(2n) time. With the cache it is O(n). The iterative version is O(n) time and O(1) space, so it is usually the best answer.

Python language questions

Say each answer out loud in about 30 seconds, then open it and compare.

List vs tuple?
A list is mutable (you can change it after creation) and a tuple is immutable. Tuples are slightly faster and, being immutable and hashable, can be used as dictionary keys. Use a tuple for fixed data such as coordinates.
Mutable vs immutable types?
Mutable objects can change in place (list, dict, set). Immutable ones cannot (int, float, str, tuple, frozenset). "Changing" an immutable value really creates a new object.
What is the difference between == and is?
== checks whether two values are equal. is checks whether two names point to the very same object in memory. Use is mainly for None checks (x is None).
Why is def f(x=[]) dangerous?
The default list is created once, when the function is defined, and shared by every call. Appending to it in one call changes what later calls see. The fix is def f(x=None): and then if x is None: x = [] inside.
Shallow copy vs deep copy?
A shallow copy (list.copy(), copy.copy) copies the outer container but shares the inner objects. A deep copy (copy.deepcopy) copies everything recursively. It matters for nested lists: changing an inner list through a shallow copy changes the original too.
What is a generator?
A function that uses yield to produce values one at a time instead of building a whole list. It saves memory for big or endless sequences, because only one value exists at a time.
What is a decorator?
A function that takes another function and returns a wrapped version of it, adding behaviour such as logging or timing without editing the original. It is applied with the @name syntax above a function.
What is the GIL?
The Global Interpreter Lock in CPython lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time. Threads are still useful for I/O-bound work such as network calls, but CPU-bound work needs multiprocessing to use several cores.

Day 1Module 2, about 60 minutes

Stack and queue

A stack is last in, first out (LIFO), like a pile of plates. A queue is first in, first out (FIFO), like a ticket counter line. Interviewers ask you to build both because it shows you understand how data structures work underneath.

In Python, a plain list works well as a stack because append() and pop() at the end are O(1). It is a poor queue, because pop(0) shifts every element and costs O(n). For a queue use collections.deque, where append() and popleft() are both O(1).

Worked example: a stack

class Stack:
    def __init__(self):
        self._items = []

    def push(self, x):
        self._items.append(x)

    def pop(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("pop from empty stack")
        return self._items.pop()

    def peek(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("peek from empty stack")
        return self._items[-1]

    def is_empty(self):
        return len(self._items) == 0

    def size(self):
        return len(self._items)

Three things an interviewer looks for: the underscore in _items shows you understand encapsulation, the empty case is handled explicitly, and every method is O(1).

Try it: Build a queue from scratch

Priority

Write a Queue class with enqueue(x), dequeue(), peek(), is_empty() and size(). Then answer in words:

  1. Why deque and not a list?
  2. What is the time complexity of each method?
  3. How does your dequeue() behave on an empty queue, and why did you choose that?
Show solution and explanation
from collections import deque

class Queue:
    def __init__(self):
        self._items = deque()

    def enqueue(self, x):
        self._items.append(x)

    def dequeue(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("dequeue from empty queue")
        return self._items.popleft()

    def peek(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("peek from empty queue")
        return self._items[0]

    def is_empty(self):
        return len(self._items) == 0

    def size(self):
        return len(self._items)

1. Why deque. list.pop(0) is O(n) because every remaining element shifts left. deque.popleft() is O(1).

2. Complexity. All five methods are O(1).

3. Empty queue. Raising IndexError makes the bug visible immediately. Returning None is also acceptable, but then callers must remember to check, and a real None stored in the queue becomes ambiguous. Say which you chose and give the reason, since that is what gets scored.

Try it: Valid parentheses

Priority

Given a string containing only ()[]{}, return True if every bracket is closed by the correct type in the correct order.

is_valid("()[]{}")   # True
is_valid("{[()]}")   # True
is_valid("(]")       # False
is_valid("(((")      # False

Hint: what is the last opening bracket you have seen that is still unclosed?

Show solution and explanation
def is_valid(s):
    pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    stack = []
    for ch in s:
        if ch in pairs:                        # a closing bracket
            if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:
                return False
        else:                                  # an opening bracket
            stack.append(ch)
    return not stack                           # leftovers mean unclosed

Idea: push every opening bracket. When a closing bracket arrives, it must match the most recent unclosed opening one, which is the top of the stack.

Walkthrough for {[()]}: push {, push [, push (. Then ) pops (, a match. ] pops [, a match. } pops {, a match. The stack is empty, so the answer is True.

Edge cases: a closing bracket first ("]", stack empty, so False), and leftover openers at the end ("(((", so the final return not stack gives False). Time O(n), space O(n).

Try it: Min stack

Design a stack that supports push, pop, top and get_min, where get_min returns the smallest element in O(1) time.

Hint: what extra information can you store with each element so the minimum survives pops?

Show solution and explanation
class MinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self._stack = []          # each entry is (value, minimum so far)

    def push(self, x):
        current_min = min(x, self._stack[-1][1]) if self._stack else x
        self._stack.append((x, current_min))

    def pop(self):
        return self._stack.pop()[0]

    def top(self):
        return self._stack[-1][0]

    def get_min(self):
        return self._stack[-1][1]

Each entry stores the value and the minimum of everything at or below it. When you pop, the previous entry still knows its own minimum, so nothing needs recomputing. Every operation is O(1), and space is O(n).

Try it: Queue using two stacks

A classic follow-up. Build a queue using only two stacks (Python lists, using only append and pop at the end).

Hint: pouring one stack into another reverses the order.

Show solution and explanation
class QueueWithStacks:
    def __init__(self):
        self._in = []
        self._out = []

    def enqueue(self, x):
        self._in.append(x)

    def dequeue(self):
        if not self._out:                      # refill only when empty
            while self._in:
                self._out.append(self._in.pop())
        if not self._out:
            raise IndexError("dequeue from empty queue")
        return self._out.pop()

Push new items onto the _in stack. When you need to dequeue and _out is empty, pour everything from _in into _out. That reverses the order, so the oldest item is now on top. Each element moves at most once, so dequeue is amortized O(1): occasionally slow, but O(1) on average over many operations.

Stack and queue questions

Say each answer out loud in about 30 seconds, then open it and compare.

Where are stacks used in real systems?
The function call stack (each call is pushed, and returns pop it), undo in editors, browser back button, bracket matching in compilers, and depth-first search.
Where are queues used in real systems?
Printer job queues, task scheduling, message queues between services, breadth-first search, and CPU scheduling such as round robin.
Why is list.pop(0) slow in Python?
A list is a contiguous array. Removing the first element shifts all the others one position left, which is O(n). A deque is built for cheap operations at both ends.
Array-based vs linked-list-based stack?
An array-based stack has good cache behaviour and simple code, but may need to resize. A linked-list stack grows one node at a time with no resizing, but uses extra memory for pointers. Both give O(1) push and pop.
What is a circular queue and why use it?
A fixed-size array where the front and rear indices wrap around to the start. It reuses freed space and avoids shifting elements, so both operations stay O(1) with no wasted slots.
What is a priority queue?
A queue where the item with the highest priority leaves first, not the oldest. It is usually built on a heap. In Python use heapq, where push and pop are O(log n).

Day 1Module 3, about 60 minutes

Hashmaps

A hashmap (Python's dict and set) turns a key into a storage position using a hash function, so lookup, insert and delete are O(1) on average. Different keys can land on the same position (a collision), which Python resolves by probing for another free slot. In the worst case with many collisions, operations degrade to O(n), but that is rare.

Keys must be hashable, meaning immutable: strings, numbers and tuples work, but lists do not.

Most hashmap problems follow one of three patterns:

  • Seen before? Remember what you have met so far, so a repeat or a needed partner is found instantly.
  • Counting. How many times does each item appear?
  • Grouping. Put items that share a key into the same bucket.

Try it: Two sum

Priority

Given a list of numbers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Assume exactly one answer exists.

two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9)   # [0, 1], because 2 + 7 = 9

Do it in two steps, the way you would in the interview: first write the brute force and state its complexity, then improve it with a dictionary.

Show solution and explanation

Brute force: check every pair. Time O(n²), space O(1).

def two_sum_brute(nums, target):
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(nums)):
            if nums[i] + nums[j] == target:
                return [i, j]
    return []

Optimized: as you walk the list, ask "have I already seen the number that completes this one?" If yes, you are done.

def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}                        # value -> index
    for i, n in enumerate(nums):
        need = target - n
        if need in seen:
            return [seen[need], i]
        seen[n] = i
    return []

Walkthrough on [2, 7, 11, 15], target 9:

  • i=0, n=2, need 7. Not in seen yet, so store {2: 0}.
  • i=1, n=7, need 2. It is in seen at index 0, so return [0, 1].

Time O(n), space O(n). This is the trade you should say out loud: extra memory for speed. Check need in seen before storing the current number, so a number is never paired with itself.

Try it: Four quick hashmap problems

Priority

Write each one:

  1. is_anagram(a, b): do two strings use exactly the same letters with the same counts?
  2. has_duplicate(nums): does any value appear twice?
  3. group_anagrams(words): ["eat","tea","tan","ate","nat","bat"] becomes [["eat","tea","ate"],["tan","nat"],["bat"]].
  4. top_k_frequent(nums, k): the k most common values.
Show solution and explanation
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

def is_anagram(a, b):
    return Counter(a) == Counter(b)

def has_duplicate(nums):
    return len(set(nums)) != len(nums)

def group_anagrams(words):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for w in words:
        groups["".join(sorted(w))].append(w)
    return list(groups.values())

def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    return [n for n, _ in Counter(nums).most_common(k)]
  • Anagram: two Counters are equal when every letter has the same count. O(n).
  • Duplicate: a set drops repeats, so a shorter set means a duplicate existed. O(n).
  • Group anagrams: words that are anagrams share the same sorted letters, so that sorted string is the dictionary key. If the longest word has length L, this costs O(n · L log L).
  • Top k: most_common(k) is roughly O(n log k). A bucket approach (index = frequency) can reach O(n), which is a nice follow-up to mention.

Hashmap questions

Say each answer out loud in about 30 seconds, then open it and compare.

How does a hash table work?
A hash function converts the key into an integer, which is mapped to a slot in an underlying array. Lookup computes the same hash and jumps straight to that slot, so on average it takes O(1) time regardless of size.
What is a collision and how is it handled?
A collision is two different keys mapping to the same slot. Chaining stores a small list of entries in each slot. Open addressing (used by Python's dict) probes for the next free slot. Both stay fast as long as the table is not too full, which is why tables resize as they grow.
Why can't a list be a dictionary key?
Keys must be hashable, and a hash must never change. A list is mutable, so its contents (and hash) could change after insertion and the dictionary could never find it again. Use a tuple instead.
dict vs set?
A dict maps keys to values. A set stores only unique keys with no values. Both give O(1) average membership checks.
What is the worst-case time of a dict lookup?
O(n), if all keys collide into the same place. With a good hash function this is very unlikely, so we quote O(1) average.
When would you not use a hashmap?
When you need the data in sorted order (use a sorted list or tree), when memory is very tight, or when the keys have no good hash function.

Day 1Module 4, about 75 minutes

Arrays, strings and two pointers

Array and string problems reuse a small set of patterns. Learn to recognise them:

PatternUse it whenExample below
Two pointersWorking from both ends, or one slow and one fast pointerValid palindrome, move zeroes
Sliding windowA contiguous stretch that grows and shrinksLongest substring without repeats
Track a running bestOne pass while remembering the best so farStock profit, max subarray
Sort firstOrder makes neighbours easy to compareMerge intervals

Try it: Valid palindrome

Priority

Return True if a string reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring case and anything that is not a letter or digit.

is_palindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama")   # True
is_palindrome("race a car")                        # False

Hint: put one pointer at each end and move them towards each other. Try to do it without building a cleaned copy of the string.

Show solution and explanation
def is_palindrome(s):
    left, right = 0, len(s) - 1
    while left < right:
        while left < right and not s[left].isalnum():
            left += 1
        while left < right and not s[right].isalnum():
            right -= 1
        if s[left].lower() != s[right].lower():
            return False
        left += 1
        right -= 1
    return True

Skip non-alphanumeric characters on each side, then compare the two characters case-insensitively. Time O(n), space O(1). The simpler version t = "".join(c.lower() for c in s if c.isalnum()); return t == t[::-1] is also fine (O(n) space), and worth mentioning as the quick option.

Try it: Best time to buy and sell a stock

prices[i] is the price on day i. Buy once, sell later, and return the maximum profit (0 if no profit is possible).

max_profit([7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4])   # 5  (buy at 1, sell at 6)
max_profit([7, 6, 4, 3, 1])      # 0
Show solution and explanation
def max_profit(prices):
    lowest = float("inf")
    best = 0
    for p in prices:
        lowest = min(lowest, p)             # cheapest day so far
        best = max(best, p - lowest)        # sell today?
    return best

Walk through the days once, remembering the lowest price seen so far. On each day ask: "if I sold today, having bought at the cheapest earlier day, what would I make?" Keep the best answer. Time O(n), space O(1). The brute force checks every buy/sell pair in O(n²).

Try it: Maximum subarray (Kadane's algorithm)

Priority

Find the largest sum of any contiguous part of a list that may contain negatives.

max_subarray([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4])   # 6  (the part [4, -1, 2, 1])
max_subarray([-3, -1, -2])                        # -1
Show solution and explanation
def max_subarray(nums):
    best = current = nums[0]
    for n in nums[1:]:
        current = max(n, current + n)       # extend, or start fresh at n
        best = max(best, current)
    return best

At each number you have two choices: extend the running subarray, or start a new one at this number. If the running sum so far is negative, it only hurts, so starting fresh is better. current holds the best sum ending here, and best holds the best seen anywhere. Time O(n), space O(1).

Start with nums[0], not 0, so an all-negative list still returns the correct (negative) answer.

Try it: Longest substring without repeating characters

Priority

Return the length of the longest stretch of the string with no repeated character.

length_of_longest_substring("abcabcbb")   # 3  ("abc")
length_of_longest_substring("bbbbb")         # 1
length_of_longest_substring("pwwkew")         # 3  ("wke")

Hint: keep a window [start, i] with no repeats. When a repeat appears, slide the left edge past the earlier copy.

Show solution and explanation
def length_of_longest_substring(s):
    last_seen = {}
    start = 0                               # left edge of the window
    best = 0
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last_seen and last_seen[ch] >= start:
            start = last_seen[ch] + 1       # jump past the repeat
        last_seen[ch] = i
        best = max(best, i - start + 1)
    return best

The dictionary remembers the last index of each character. When the current character was last seen inside the window (last_seen[ch] >= start), move start just past that earlier copy. The window length is i - start + 1.

The trap: the >= start check. In "abba", when the final a arrives, its old position (0) is already outside the window, so you must not move start backwards. Try it by hand. Time O(n), space O(k) for k distinct characters.

Try it: Merge intervals

Merge all overlapping intervals.

merge_intervals([[1,3],[8,10],[2,6],[15,18]])   # [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]
Show solution and explanation
def merge_intervals(intervals):
    intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    merged = []
    for start, end in intervals:
        if merged and start <= merged[-1][1]:       # overlaps the last one
            merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], end)
        else:
            merged.append([start, end])
    return merged

Sort by start time. Then each interval either overlaps the last merged one (its start is at or before that one's end, so extend the end) or does not (start a new one). Sorting dominates: O(n log n). This "sort first, then sweep" pattern shows up constantly, for example with meeting rooms or transaction time windows.

Try it: Move zeroes to the end

Move every 0 to the end of the list in place, keeping the order of the non-zero values.

move_zeroes([0, 1, 0, 3, 12])   # [1, 3, 12, 0, 0]
Show solution and explanation
def move_zeroes(nums):
    write = 0
    for read in range(len(nums)):
        if nums[read] != 0:
            nums[write], nums[read] = nums[read], nums[write]
            write += 1
    return nums

Two pointers: read scans every element, and write marks where the next non-zero value belongs. Swapping non-zero values forward pushes zeroes to the back. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

Day 1Module 5, about 60 minutes

Linked lists

A linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. Unlike an array, elements are not next to each other in memory.

Array / listLinked list
Access the i-th itemO(1)O(n), you must walk from the head
Insert or delete at the frontO(n)O(1)
Insert or delete in the middleO(n)O(1) once you hold the node before it, but finding that node is O(n)
MemoryCompactExtra pointer per node

Use this small setup for every exercise below. from_list and to_list are just helpers so you can test your code.

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

def from_list(values):                 # helper: build a list to test with
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    for v in values:
        tail.next = ListNode(v)
        tail = tail.next
    return dummy.next

def to_list(head):                     # helper: turn it back into a Python list
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

Try it: Build a singly linked list

Priority

Write a SinglyLinkedList class using ListNode, with append(val), prepend(val), delete(val) (delete the first node with that value; return True if found) and to_list().

Think about the special cases before coding: empty list, deleting the head, deleting the last node, value not found.

Show solution and explanation
class SinglyLinkedList:
    def __init__(self):
        self.head = None

    def append(self, val):
        node = ListNode(val)
        if self.head is None:
            self.head = node
            return
        curr = self.head
        while curr.next:
            curr = curr.next
        curr.next = node

    def prepend(self, val):
        self.head = ListNode(val, self.head)

    def delete(self, val):
        if self.head is None:
            return False
        if self.head.val == val:
            self.head = self.head.next
            return True
        curr = self.head
        while curr.next:
            if curr.next.val == val:
                curr.next = curr.next.next
                return True
            curr = curr.next
        return False

    def to_list(self):
        return to_list(self.head)

append walks to the last node: O(n). prepend is O(1). delete keeps a pointer to the node before the one being removed, so it can skip over it with curr.next = curr.next.next. The head is a special case because it has no previous node.

Try it: Four classic linked-list functions

Priority

Write each, using ListNode and the helpers above:

  1. reverse_list(head): reverse the list and return the new head.
  2. has_cycle(head): does the list loop back on itself?
  3. middle_node(head): return the middle node (the second of the two middles for even lengths).
  4. merge_two_lists(a, b): merge two sorted lists into one sorted list.

Hint for 2 and 3: use two pointers moving at different speeds.

Show solution and explanation
def reverse_list(head):
    prev = None
    curr = head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next          # 1. remember the rest
        curr.next = prev         # 2. flip the pointer
        prev = curr              # 3. move prev forward
        curr = nxt               # 4. move curr forward
    return prev

def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            return True
    return False

def middle_node(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    return slow

def merge_two_lists(a, b):
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val:
            tail.next = a
            a = a.next
        else:
            tail.next = b
            b = b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a or b           # attach whichever list still has nodes
    return dummy.next
  • Reverse: for each node, remember the rest, flip its pointer backwards, then step forward. Four lines you should be able to write on demand. O(n) time, O(1) space.
  • Cycle (Floyd's tortoise and hare): slow moves one step, fast two. If there is a loop, fast eventually laps slow and they meet. If there is no loop, fast reaches the end. O(n) time, O(1) space, versus O(n) space for a "visited" set.
  • Middle: when fast reaches the end, slow is halfway, since it moved half as far.
  • Merge: a dummy head node avoids special-casing the first node. Repeatedly attach the smaller front node. When one list runs out, attach the rest of the other. O(n + m).

Linked list questions

Say each answer out loud in about 30 seconds, then open it and compare.

Array vs linked list: when do you pick each?
Pick an array when you need fast access by index or a compact memory layout. Pick a linked list when you insert and delete a lot at known positions (especially the front) and rarely index.
Singly vs doubly linked list?
A doubly linked list has a pointer back to the previous node as well. That allows walking in both directions and O(1) deletion of a node you hold, at the cost of more memory per node.
How do you find the start of a cycle?
After slow and fast meet, reset one pointer to the head. Move both one step at a time. They meet again at the node where the cycle begins.
How do you delete a node when you are only given that node (not the head)?
Copy the next node's value into this node, then link past the next node: node.val = node.next.val; node.next = node.next.next. It does not work for the last node.
How would you detect a palindrome linked list in O(1) extra space?
Find the middle with slow and fast pointers, reverse the second half, then compare the two halves node by node. Optionally reverse it back afterwards.

Day 1Module 6, about 75 minutes

Binary search, sorting and trees

Binary search

If the data is sorted, you do not need to look at every item. Check the middle: if it is your target, you are done; if the target is bigger, discard the left half; otherwise discard the right half. The range halves each step, so the time is O(log n). For a million items, that is about 20 steps.

Try it: Binary search

Priority

Write binary_search(nums, target) for a sorted list. Return the index, or -1 if it is not there. Do not use the built-in index or bisect.

Show solution and explanation
def binary_search(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1                 # target is in the right half
        else:
            hi = mid - 1                 # target is in the left half
    return -1

The loop runs while lo <= hi, so a one-element range is still checked. After a comparison you move lo or hi to mid + 1 or mid - 1, never leaving them at mid, which could loop forever.

Test with: an empty list, one element, the first element, the last element, and a value that is missing. Off-by-one errors live at exactly those places.

Try it: Search insert position

Given a sorted list and a target, return the index where the target is found, or where it would be inserted to keep the list sorted.

search_insert([1, 3, 5, 6], 5)   # 2
search_insert([1, 3, 5, 6], 2)   # 1
search_insert([1, 3, 5, 6], 7)   # 4
Show solution and explanation
def search_insert(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums)                # hi = len, because we may insert at the end
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo

This version uses a half-open range [lo, hi), with hi = len(nums) because inserting at the very end is a valid answer. It finds the first position whose value is greater than or equal to the target. This is exactly what Python's bisect.bisect_left does, so you can mention it as the library shortcut.

Sorting

AlgorithmBestAverageWorstExtra spaceStable?
BubbleO(n)O(n²)O(n²)O(1)Yes
SelectionO(n²)O(n²)O(n²)O(1)No
InsertionO(n)O(n²)O(n²)O(1)Yes
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)O(n log n)O(n)Yes
QuickO(n log n)O(n log n)O(n²)O(log n)No
HeapO(n log n)O(n log n)O(n log n)O(1)No

A sort is stable if equal items keep their original relative order. Python's built-in sorted() and list.sort() use Timsort, which is O(n log n) and stable.

Try it: Merge sort

Write merge_sort(arr) that returns a new sorted list. Idea: split in half, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves.

Show solution and explanation
def merge_sort(arr):
    if len(arr) <= 1:
        return arr
    mid = len(arr) // 2
    left = merge_sort(arr[:mid])
    right = merge_sort(arr[mid:])
    merged = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            merged.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            merged.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    merged.extend(left[i:])
    merged.extend(right[j:])
    return merged

The base case is a list of 0 or 1 items, which is already sorted. The merge step walks two pointers, always taking the smaller front item; <= (not <) keeps equal items in their original order, making it stable. There are log n levels of splitting, and each level does O(n) merging work, so O(n log n) overall, with O(n) extra space.

Trees

A binary tree node has up to two children. A binary search tree (BST) adds a rule: everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node, and everything in the right subtree is larger. That makes search, insert and delete O(height), which is O(log n) if the tree is balanced but O(n) if it degenerates into a chain.

The four traversals, on a tree with root 8, children 3 and 10:

  • Inorder (left, node, right): gives a BST's values in sorted order.
  • Preorder (node, left, right): useful for copying a tree.
  • Postorder (left, right, node): useful for deleting a tree.
  • Level order (breadth-first): one level at a time, using a queue.

Try it: BST insert, traversal, height

Priority

Write a TreeNode class, then:

  1. bst_insert(root, val), returning the root
  2. inorder(root), returning a list
  3. height(root), where an empty tree has height 0
  4. level_order(root), returning a list of levels

Insert 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14 and check that inorder gives [1, 3, 6, 8, 10, 14], height is 3, and level order is [[8], [3, 10], [1, 6, 14]].

Show solution and explanation
from collections import deque

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def bst_insert(root, val):
    if root is None:
        return TreeNode(val)
    if val < root.val:
        root.left = bst_insert(root.left, val)
    else:
        root.right = bst_insert(root.right, val)
    return root

def inorder(root):                       # left, node, right -> sorted for a BST
    if root is None:
        return []
    return inorder(root.left) + [root.val] + inorder(root.right)

def height(root):
    if root is None:
        return 0
    return 1 + max(height(root.left), height(root.right))

def level_order(root):                   # breadth-first, one level at a time
    if root is None:
        return []
    result, queue = [], deque([root])
    while queue:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(queue)):
            node = queue.popleft()
            level.append(node.val)
            if node.left:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                queue.append(node.right)
        result.append(level)
    return result

Insert, inorder and height are naturally recursive: solve for the left and right subtrees, then combine. Level order is not recursive. It uses a deque as a queue and processes exactly len(queue) nodes per level, which is what separates the levels. All four are O(n) except insert, which is O(height).

Sorting, search and tree questions

Say each answer out loud in about 30 seconds, then open it and compare.

Quicksort vs merge sort?
Merge sort always takes O(n log n), is stable, and needs O(n) extra space. Quicksort is usually faster in practice and sorts in place, but its worst case is O(n²) (for example, an already sorted array with a bad pivot choice) and it is not stable.
Which sort would you use for a nearly sorted list?
Insertion sort, which is close to O(n) on nearly sorted data. In practice, Python's Timsort already exploits that.
What is the worst case for a BST and how do you avoid it?
Inserting sorted data creates a chain, so operations take O(n). Self-balancing trees such as AVL or red-black trees rotate nodes to keep the height around O(log n).
DFS vs BFS?
Depth-first search goes as deep as possible before backtracking, using a stack or recursion. Breadth-first search explores level by level, using a queue, and finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
What does inorder traversal of a BST give?
The values in sorted ascending order.
What is a heap?
A complete binary tree in which every parent is smaller than (min-heap) or larger than (max-heap) its children. The smallest or largest element is always at the root, and push and pop are O(log n). It powers priority queues.
Why is binary search O(log n)?
Each step discards half the remaining range. The number of times you can halve n before reaching 1 is log₂ n.

Day 1Module 7, about 60 minutes

Object-oriented programming

OOP questions are guaranteed in a fresher interview. The safest approach is to answer each one with a definition and a small example. The bank-account example below fits HSBC perfectly, and you can reuse it for every question.

The four pillars in plain words

PillarMeaningBank-account example
EncapsulationBundle data with the methods that use it, and control access to itThe balance is stored internally and changed only through deposit and withdraw, which check the rules
AbstractionShow what something does, hide how it does itYou call withdraw(500) without knowing how overdraft checks work inside
InheritanceA class reuses and extends another classSavingsAccount and CurrentAccount both inherit from Account
PolymorphismOne interface, many behavioursCalling describe() on any account works, and each type answers in its own way

Try it: Build the account hierarchy

Priority

Design these classes, then use them:

  • An abstract base class Account with an owner and a balance, deposit(amount) (reject amounts that are not positive), withdraw(amount), and a describe() method.
  • withdraw must reject a request that goes beyond the balance plus the account's overdraft limit. Each account type decides its own limit through an abstract method.
  • SavingsAccount allows no overdraft. CurrentAccount allows 1000, and its describe() adds a note to the parent's text.
  • A class variable bank_name, and a read-only balance property.

Then create one of each, loop over both calling describe(), and check that withdrawing 600 from a Savings account with 500 fails.

Show solution and explanation
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Account(ABC):                            # abstract: cannot be created directly
    bank_name = "Demo Bank"                    # class variable: shared by all accounts

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner                     # instance variables: one copy per object
        self._balance = balance                # leading underscore: "internal, don't touch"

    @property
    def balance(self):                         # read-only access from outside
        return self._balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("amount must be positive")
        self._balance += amount

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount > self._balance + self.overdraft_limit():
            raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
        self._balance -= amount

    @abstractmethod
    def overdraft_limit(self):                 # every subclass MUST implement this
        ...

    def describe(self):
        return f"{type(self).__name__} of {self.owner}: {self._balance}"


class SavingsAccount(Account):
    def overdraft_limit(self):                 # overriding
        return 0


class CurrentAccount(Account):
    def overdraft_limit(self):
        return 1000

    def describe(self):                        # overriding + reusing the parent's version
        return super().describe() + " (overdraft allowed)"
  • Abstract class: Account inherits from ABC and has an @abstractmethod, so Account("x") raises TypeError. Subclasses must implement overdraft_limit.
  • Encapsulation: _balance is marked internal by the underscore, and outside code reads it through the balance property. Python does not enforce privacy, but the convention is universal.
  • Polymorphism: withdraw is written once, yet behaves differently per account type because it calls self.overdraft_limit().
  • Overriding: both subclasses replace overdraft_limit, and CurrentAccount.describe reuses the parent's version through super().
  • Class vs instance variables: bank_name belongs to the class and is shared. owner and _balance belong to each object.

Try it: Overloading, class methods and static methods

Answer these by writing code, not by explaining:

  1. Python has no true method overloading. Show how you would make an add method that accepts 2 or 3 or any number of arguments.
  2. Show a classmethod used as an alternative constructor, and a staticmethod. When would you pick each?
Show solution and explanation
class Calculator:
    def add(self, *args):                      # Python's version of "overloading"
        return sum(args)

Calculator().add(1, 2)          # 3
Calculator().add(1, 2, 3)       # 6


class Employee:
    company = "Demo Bank"
    count = 0

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        Employee.count += 1

    @classmethod
    def from_string(cls, text):                # gets the class, used as an alternative constructor
        return cls(text.split("-")[0])

    @staticmethod
    def is_valid_name(name):                   # gets neither self nor cls
        return name.isalpha()
  • Overloading: if you define two methods with the same name, the second silently replaces the first. Python's answer is default arguments or *args.
  • classmethod receives the class (cls) and is ideal for alternative constructors like from_string. It also works correctly with subclasses.
  • staticmethod receives neither the object nor the class. It is just a function that lives in the class's namespace because it belongs logically with it.

OOP questions

Say each answer out loud in about 30 seconds, then open it and compare.

Explain the four pillars of OOP.
Encapsulation: bundle data and the methods that act on it, and control access. Abstraction: expose what an object does, hide how. Inheritance: a child class reuses and extends a parent. Polymorphism: the same call behaves differently depending on the object. Give the bank-account example for each.
Abstraction vs encapsulation?
Abstraction is about the design: showing only the essential interface. Encapsulation is about the implementation: keeping the data and the code that manipulates it together, with controlled access. Abstraction hides complexity; encapsulation protects state.
Method overloading vs overriding?
Overloading is several methods with the same name and different parameters, decided at compile time (Java, C++). Python does not support it directly. Overriding is a subclass replacing a parent's method with the same signature, decided at runtime. It is how polymorphism works.
Abstract class vs interface?
An abstract class can hold both implemented methods and abstract ones, plus state. An interface (in Java) only declares behaviour, and a class can implement many of them. Python has no interface keyword. It uses ABC with abstract methods, or duck typing.
Inheritance vs composition?
Inheritance models an "is-a" relationship (a savings account is an account). Composition models "has-a" (a bank has accounts). Prefer composition when the relationship is not truly is-a, because inheritance couples the child tightly to the parent.
What are self and __init__?
Inside a method, self is the object the method was called on. __init__ is the initializer that runs right after an object is created, setting up its instance variables. It is commonly called the constructor.
Class variable vs instance variable?
A class variable is defined on the class and shared by all instances. An instance variable is set on self and belongs to one object. Changing a class variable through the class affects everyone.
Does Python have private variables?
Not truly. A single underscore (_x) signals "internal use". A double underscore (__x) triggers name mangling, which makes accidental access harder but is not real security.
What is duck typing?
If an object has the methods you call, it works, no matter its class: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck." It is Python's informal version of polymorphism.
Does Python support multiple inheritance?
Yes. When several parents define the same method, Python follows the Method Resolution Order (MRO), computed by the C3 algorithm. You can inspect it with ClassName.__mro__.

Day 2Module 8, about 150 minutes

More DSA problems with solutions

These are the problems that show up most often in campus coding rounds, grouped by topic. Each has a difficulty tag. Work in order within a topic, and use the 20-minute rule. If you are short on time, do the Priority ones first, since they cover the most common patterns.

Which technique for which problem?

The hardest part of a new problem is choosing the approach. Use the wording of the problem as a clue:

If the problem says...Think about...
find a pair, a complement, a duplicate, or count occurrencesHashmap or set
sorted array, or "find the position"Binary search, or two pointers
contiguous subarray or substringSliding window, or prefix sums
do it in place, or remove or move itemsTwo pointers (a read pointer and a write pointer)
next greater element, matching brackets, nested structureStack
middle, cycle, or n-th from the end of a linked listFast and slow pointers
top k, k-th largest or smallestHeap
level by level, or shortest path with equal costsBFS (queue)
explore everything, or connected regionsDFS (recursion or stack)
count the ways, or best result from a series of choices, with repeated sub-questionsDynamic programming

Arrays

Try it: Remove duplicates from a sorted array

EasyPriority

Remove duplicates from a sorted list in place, so each value appears once. Return the number of unique values k. The first k slots must hold the unique values in order. Do not create a new list.

a = [1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3]
remove_duplicates(a)   # 3, and a[:3] is [1, 2, 3]
Show solution and explanation
def remove_duplicates(nums):
    if not nums:
        return 0
    write = 1                                   # next slot for a new unique value
    for read in range(1, len(nums)):
        if nums[read] != nums[write - 1]:
            nums[write] = nums[read]
            write += 1
    return write

Because the list is sorted, duplicates sit next to each other. read scans every element, and write marks the next free slot for a new unique value. A value is new if it differs from the last value written. Time O(n), space O(1).

Try it: Missing number

EasyPriority

A list holds n distinct numbers taken from 0..n, so exactly one number in that range is missing. Find it.

missing_number([3, 0, 1])   # 2

Try to do it in O(n) time and O(1) space. Hint: what should the total of 0..n be?

Show solution and explanation
def missing_number(nums):                       # nums holds 0..n with one value missing
    n = len(nums)
    return n * (n + 1) // 2 - sum(nums)

The sum of 0..n is n(n+1)/2. Subtract the actual sum and what is left is the missing number. An alternative that avoids any overflow worry in other languages is XOR (see the bits problems below). Time O(n), space O(1).

Try it: Majority element

Easy

Find the value that appears more than n/2 times in a list (it always exists). Aim for O(1) extra space.

majority_element([2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2])   # 2
Show solution and explanation
def majority_element(nums):                     # the value that appears more than n/2 times
    candidate, count = None, 0
    for n in nums:
        if count == 0:
            candidate = n
        count += 1 if n == candidate else -1
    return candidate

This is the Boyer-Moore voting idea. Keep a candidate and a counter. The same value adds 1, a different value subtracts 1, and at zero you pick a new candidate. Since the majority value outnumbers all others combined, it cannot be cancelled out entirely. Time O(n), space O(1). The easy alternative is Counter(nums).most_common(1), which is O(n) space. Mention both.

Try it: Product of array except self

MediumPriority

Return a list where element i is the product of all elements except nums[i]. Do not use division.

product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4])   # [24, 12, 8, 6]

Hint: the answer for position i is (product of everything to its left) times (product of everything to its right).

Show solution and explanation
def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    result = [1] * n
    prefix = 1
    for i in range(n):                          # result[i] = product of everything left of i
        result[i] = prefix
        prefix *= nums[i]
    suffix = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):              # multiply in everything right of i
        result[i] *= suffix
        suffix *= nums[i]
    return result

The first pass stores, in result[i], the product of everything to the left of i. The second pass, going right to left, multiplies in the product of everything to the right. No division, so zeroes in the input are handled correctly. Time O(n), and O(1) extra space apart from the output list.

Try it: Rotate an array by k

Medium

Rotate a list to the right by k places, in place.

rotate([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], 3)   # [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4]
Show solution and explanation
def rotate(nums, k):                            # rotate right by k, in place
    if not nums:
        return nums
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n

    def reverse(lo, hi):
        while lo < hi:
            nums[lo], nums[hi] = nums[hi], nums[lo]
            lo += 1
            hi -= 1

    reverse(0, n - 1)                           # reverse everything
    reverse(0, k - 1)                           # then the first k
    reverse(k, n - 1)                           # then the rest
    return nums

The neat trick is three reversals: reverse the whole list, then reverse the first k, then reverse the rest. Take k %= n first, since rotating by n changes nothing. Time O(n), space O(1). The one-liner nums[:] = nums[-k:] + nums[:-k] is also fine, but it uses O(n) extra space.

Try it: Sort colors (Dutch national flag)

Medium

A list contains only 0, 1 and 2. Sort it in place in a single pass, without using sort().

sort_colors([2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0])   # [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]
Show solution and explanation
def sort_colors(nums):                          # values are only 0, 1, 2
    low, mid, high = 0, 0, len(nums) - 1
    while mid <= high:
        if nums[mid] == 0:
            nums[low], nums[mid] = nums[mid], nums[low]
            low += 1
            mid += 1
        elif nums[mid] == 1:
            mid += 1
        else:
            nums[mid], nums[high] = nums[high], nums[mid]
            high -= 1                           # do not advance mid: the swapped value is unchecked
    return nums

Three pointers split the list into regions: everything before low is 0, everything from low to before mid is 1, and everything after high is 2. Inspect nums[mid]: a 0 swaps to the front, a 1 stays, and a 2 swaps to the back. When you swap with high, do not advance mid, because the value swapped in is still unchecked. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.

Try it: Subarray sum equals k

MediumPriority

Count the contiguous subarrays whose sum is exactly k. The list may contain negative numbers.

subarray_sum([1, 1, 1], 2)   # 2
subarray_sum([1, 2, 3], 3)   # 2   ([1, 2] and [3])

Hint: with a running (prefix) sum, a subarray ending here sums to k if some earlier prefix equals running - k.

Show solution and explanation
from collections import defaultdict

def subarray_sum(nums, k):                      # how many contiguous subarrays add up to k
    counts = defaultdict(int)
    counts[0] = 1                               # the empty prefix
    running = 0
    total = 0
    for n in nums:
        running += n
        total += counts[running - k]            # earlier prefixes that leave exactly k
        counts[running] += 1
    return total

Let running be the sum of everything so far. A subarray that ends at the current element and adds up to k exists for every earlier prefix whose sum was running - k, because removing that prefix leaves exactly k. The dictionary counts how many times each prefix sum has occurred. Seeding counts[0] = 1 covers subarrays that start at index 0. Time O(n), space O(n). The brute force checks every pair of start and end in O(n²), and sliding window does not work here because of negative numbers.

Try it: 3Sum

Medium

Find all unique triplets in a list that add up to 0.

three_sum([-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4])   # [[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]
Show solution and explanation
def three_sum(nums):
    nums.sort()
    result = []
    for i in range(len(nums) - 2):
        if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
            continue                            # skip repeated first numbers
        lo, hi = i + 1, len(nums) - 1
        while lo < hi:
            s = nums[i] + nums[lo] + nums[hi]
            if s < 0:
                lo += 1
            elif s > 0:
                hi -= 1
            else:
                result.append([nums[i], nums[lo], nums[hi]])
                lo += 1
                hi -= 1
                while lo < hi and nums[lo] == nums[lo - 1]:
                    lo += 1                     # skip repeated second numbers
    return result

Sort the list, then fix the first number and use two pointers on the rest to find pairs that complete a zero sum: if the total is too small, move lo right, and if too big, move hi left. Skipping repeated values (for the first number and for the second) is what keeps the result unique. Time O(n²), space O(1) besides the output. This is a classic "reduce to two sum" problem, so say that out loud.

Strings and bits

Try it: Longest common prefix

EasyPriority

Return the longest prefix shared by every string in a list, or an empty string.

longest_common_prefix(["flower", "flow", "flight"])   # "fl"
longest_common_prefix(["dog", "car"])                 # ""
Show solution and explanation
def longest_common_prefix(words):
    if not words:
        return ""
    prefix = words[0]
    for w in words[1:]:
        while not w.startswith(prefix):
            prefix = prefix[:-1]                # shrink until it fits
    return prefix

Start with the first word as the prefix. For each other word, chop one letter off the end of the prefix until the word starts with it. Time O(total characters), space O(1). Watch the edge cases: an empty list, and a single word (which is its own prefix).

Try it: Reverse the words / is one string a rotation of another?

Easy

Write two short functions. reverse_words(" the sky is blue ") should give "blue is sky the", ignoring extra spaces. is_rotation("waterbottle", "erbottlewat") should be True.

Show solution and explanation
def reverse_words(s):
    return " ".join(s.split()[::-1])            # split() also drops extra spaces

def is_rotation(a, b):                          # is b a rotation of a?
    return len(a) == len(b) and b in a + a

split() with no argument splits on any run of whitespace, so the extra spaces vanish. For the rotation trick: every rotation of a appears inside a + a, so check the lengths match, then check b in a + a. Both are O(n).

Try it: Bit tricks: single number, power of two, count set bits

Easy

Three short problems on bits:

  1. Every value in a list appears twice, except one. Find it in O(n) time and O(1) space.
  2. Is n a power of two?
  3. Count the 1-bits in n.

Hint: XOR (^) of a number with itself is 0, and n & (n - 1) clears the lowest 1-bit of n.

Show solution and explanation
def single_number(nums):                        # every value appears twice except one
    result = 0
    for n in nums:
        result ^= n                             # x ^ x = 0, and x ^ 0 = x
    return result

def is_power_of_two(n):
    return n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0         # a power of two has exactly one 1-bit

def count_set_bits(n):
    count = 0
    while n:
        n &= n - 1                              # clears the lowest 1-bit
        count += 1
    return count
  • Single number: XOR all the values. Pairs cancel each other (x ^ x = 0) and 0 does not change anything, so only the unpaired value remains.
  • Power of two: a power of two in binary has exactly one 1-bit, and n & (n - 1) removes it, leaving 0. Check n > 0 too.
  • Count set bits (Brian Kernighan's method): repeat n &= n - 1, counting how many times before n becomes 0. It loops once per 1-bit.

Stacks and linked lists

Try it: Next greater element

MediumPriority

For each element, find the next element to its right that is strictly greater. Use -1 when there is none.

next_greater([2, 1, 2, 4, 3])   # [4, 2, 4, -1, -1]

Hint: keep a stack of positions that are still waiting to find something bigger.

Show solution and explanation
def next_greater(nums):
    result = [-1] * len(nums)
    stack = []                                  # indices still waiting for a bigger value
    for i, n in enumerate(nums):
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < n:
            result[stack.pop()] = n
        stack.append(i)
    return result

This is the monotonic stack pattern. The stack holds indices of values that have not yet found a greater one. When a new value arrives, it is the answer for every waiting index with a smaller value, so pop and fill those in, then push the new index. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so time is O(n) and space is O(n). The brute force is O(n²). The same pattern solves "daily temperatures" and "stock span".

Try it: Remove n-th node from the end / add two numbers as linked lists

MediumPriority

Use ListNode, from_list and to_list from the linked lists module.

  1. remove_nth_from_end(head, n): remove the n-th node counted from the end, in one pass.
  2. add_two_numbers(a, b): two numbers are stored as linked lists with digits in reverse order ([2,4,3] means 342). Return their sum in the same format.
remove_nth_from_end([1,2,3,4,5], 2)   # [1, 2, 3, 5]
add_two_numbers([2,4,3], [5,6,4])     # [7, 0, 8]   (342 + 465 = 807)
Show solution and explanation
def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)                   # dummy handles removing the head
    fast = slow = dummy
    for _ in range(n):                          # open a gap of n nodes
        fast = fast.next
    while fast.next:                            # move both until fast is at the last node
        fast = fast.next
        slow = slow.next
    slow.next = slow.next.next                  # slow is just before the target
    return dummy.next

def add_two_numbers(a, b):                      # digits stored in reverse order
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    carry = 0
    while a or b or carry:
        total = carry + (a.val if a else 0) + (b.val if b else 0)
        carry, digit = divmod(total, 10)
        tail.next = ListNode(digit)
        tail = tail.next
        a = a.next if a else None
        b = b.next if b else None
    return dummy.next
  • Remove n-th from the end: move fast n steps ahead, then move both pointers together until fast reaches the last node. Now slow sits right before the node to delete. A dummy node in front handles removing the head. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.
  • Add two numbers: walk both lists together, adding the digits and a carry. divmod(total, 10) gives the carry and the digit at once. The loop continues while either list has nodes or a carry remains, so [9,9] + [1] correctly produces [0,0,1]. Time O(max(n, m)).

Searching and heaps

Try it: Search in a rotated sorted array

MediumPriority

A sorted list of distinct values was rotated at an unknown point, for example [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]. Find the index of target in O(log n), or return -1.

search_rotated([4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], 0)   # 4
search_rotated([4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], 3)   # -1

Hint: after you split at the middle, at least one half is always properly sorted.

Show solution and explanation
def search_rotated(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[lo] <= nums[mid]:               # the left half is sorted
            if nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]:
                hi = mid - 1
            else:
                lo = mid + 1
        else:                                   # the right half is sorted
            if nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]:
                lo = mid + 1
            else:
                hi = mid - 1
    return -1

At each step, work out which half is sorted: if nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted. Then ask whether the target lies inside that sorted half's range. If yes, search that half, and if no, search the other half. Every step still discards half the range, so it is O(log n) time and O(1) space. Test with the target being the first element, the last element, the pivot, and a missing value.

Try it: K-th largest element

Medium

Return the k-th largest value in an unsorted list.

kth_largest([3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], 2)   # 5
Show solution and explanation
import heapq

def kth_largest(nums, k):
    heap = []                                   # min-heap holding the k largest seen so far
    for n in nums:
        heapq.heappush(heap, n)
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)                 # drop the smallest of the k+1
    return heap[0]

Keep a min-heap of size k that always holds the k largest values seen so far. Push each number, and if the heap grows past k, pop the smallest. At the end, the root is the k-th largest. Time O(n log k), space O(k). Compare with the simple answer, sorted(nums)[-k], which is O(n log n). The heap version wins when k is small or the data is a stream.

Trees

Use TreeNode, bst_insert and inorder from the trees module to build a tree to test with.

Try it: Invert a tree, validate a BST, lowest common ancestor

MediumPriority

Write three functions:

  1. invert_tree(root): swap the left and right children at every node.
  2. is_valid_bst(root): is this a valid binary search tree?
  3. lowest_common_ancestor(root, p, q): for a BST, the lowest node that has both values p and q beneath it.

Hint for 2: comparing a node only with its direct children is not enough. Each node must fall inside a range set by its ancestors.

Show solution and explanation
def invert_tree(root):
    if root is None:
        return None
    root.left, root.right = invert_tree(root.right), invert_tree(root.left)
    return root

def is_valid_bst(root, low=float("-inf"), high=float("inf")):
    if root is None:
        return True
    if not (low < root.val < high):             # every node must sit inside its allowed range
        return False
    return (is_valid_bst(root.left, low, root.val) and
            is_valid_bst(root.right, root.val, high))

def lowest_common_ancestor(root, p, q):         # for a BST, p and q are values
    while root:
        if p < root.val and q < root.val:
            root = root.left
        elif p > root.val and q > root.val:
            root = root.right
        else:
            return root.val                     # the paths split here
    return None
  • Invert: recursively invert both subtrees, then swap them. It is a classic quick recursion problem. Time O(n).
  • Validate BST: pass down an allowed range (low, high). Going left, the upper limit becomes the current value. Going right, the lower limit becomes the current value. The common mistake is checking only parent against child, which wrongly accepts a tree where a deep node breaks an ancestor's rule. An alternative is to check that inorder traversal is strictly increasing.
  • LCA in a BST: if both values are smaller than the current node, go left. If both are larger, go right. Otherwise, the paths split here, so this is the answer. Time O(height), space O(1).

Dynamic programming

Dynamic programming (DP) applies when a problem breaks into overlapping subproblems and the best answer is built from the best answers to smaller ones. Use this recipe every time:

  1. State: what does dp[i] mean, in words?
  2. Recurrence: how does dp[i] follow from smaller states?
  3. Base case: the smallest answers you know directly.
  4. Order: fill the table so the pieces you need already exist.
  5. Answer: which cell holds the result? Then see if you can shrink the memory.

Try it: Climbing stairs

EasyPriority

You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways are there to reach step n?

climb_stairs(1) = 1,  climb_stairs(2) = 2,  climb_stairs(3) = 3,  climb_stairs(5) = 8

Hint: to reach step n, you came from step n-1 or step n-2.

Show solution and explanation
def climb_stairs(n):                            # ways to climb n steps, taking 1 or 2 at a time
    a, b = 1, 1                                 # ways to reach step 0 and step 1
    for _ in range(n - 1):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return b

State: ways(n) is the number of ways to reach step n. Recurrence: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2), which is the Fibonacci sequence. Because only the last two values are needed, two variables replace the whole table: O(n) time and O(1) space. The plain recursion without memory would be O(2n), which is exactly why DP exists.

Try it: House robber

Medium

Houses in a row hold money, and you cannot rob two adjacent houses. What is the most you can take?

rob([1, 2, 3, 1])      # 4   (houses 1 and 3)
rob([2, 7, 9, 3, 1])   # 12  (houses 1, 3 and 5)
Show solution and explanation
def rob(nums):                                  # max money without robbing two adjacent houses
    take, skip = 0, 0                           # best total if we take / skip the current house
    for n in nums:
        take, skip = skip + n, max(take, skip)
    return max(take, skip)

At each house you choose: take it (then you must have skipped the previous one, so add to the "skip" total) or skip it (keep the best of the previous two choices). The two running variables hold those totals. The tuple assignment evaluates the right side first using the old values, which is what makes the update correct. Time O(n), space O(1).

Try it: Coin change

MediumPriority

Given coin values and a target amount, return the fewest coins that make the amount, or -1 if it is impossible. You have unlimited coins of each value.

coin_change([1, 2, 5], 11)   # 3   (5 + 5 + 1)
coin_change([2], 3)          # -1
coin_change([1, 3, 4], 6)    # 2   (3 + 3, not 4 + 1 + 1)

Watch out: always picking the biggest coin (greedy) fails on the third example.

Show solution and explanation
def coin_change(coins, amount):
    INF = float("inf")
    dp = [0] + [INF] * amount                   # dp[a] = fewest coins that make amount a
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):
        for c in coins:
            if c <= a and dp[a - c] + 1 < dp[a]:
                dp[a] = dp[a - c] + 1
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] != INF else -1

State: dp[a] is the fewest coins needed to make amount a. Recurrence: try every coin c that fits, and take dp[a - c] + 1 if it improves the best. Base case: dp[0] = 0. Unreachable amounts stay at infinity, which becomes -1 at the end. Time O(amount × number of coins), space O(amount). The third example shows why greedy is wrong and DP is needed: greedy would choose 4 first and end up with 3 coins, while the best is 2.

Try it: Longest common subsequence

Medium

Return the length of the longest subsequence (characters in order, not necessarily next to each other) that two strings share.

lcs("abcde", "ace")   # 3   ("ace")
Show solution and explanation
def lcs(a, b):                                  # length of the longest common subsequence
    dp = [[0] * (len(b) + 1) for _ in range(len(a) + 1)]
    for i in range(1, len(a) + 1):
        for j in range(1, len(b) + 1):
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1
            else:
                dp[i][j] = max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])
    return dp[len(a)][len(b)]

State: dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i characters of a and the first j characters of b. If the two current characters match, extend the best answer without them (dp[i-1][j-1] + 1). Otherwise take the better of dropping a character from either string. Time and space O(n × m). A subsequence need not be contiguous, and that is the difference from a "substring" problem.

Graphs

A graph is a set of nodes connected by edges. The usual representation in interviews is an adjacency list: a dictionary that maps each node to the list of its neighbours. It uses O(V + E) space, unlike an adjacency matrix, which uses O(V²).

Try it: BFS and DFS

MediumPriority

For graph = {"A": ["B", "C"], "B": ["D"], "C": ["D"], "D": []}, write:

  1. bfs(graph, start), returning the nodes in the order they are visited, level by level
  2. dfs(graph, node), returning the visit order going as deep as possible first
bfs(graph, "A")   # ["A", "B", "C", "D"]
dfs(graph, "A")   # ["A", "B", "D", "C"]
Show solution and explanation
from collections import deque

graph = {"A": ["B", "C"], "B": ["D"], "C": ["D"], "D": []}

def bfs(graph, start):
    seen, order, queue = {start}, [], deque([start])
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        order.append(node)
        for nxt in graph[node]:
            if nxt not in seen:
                seen.add(nxt)                   # mark when queued, so nothing is queued twice
                queue.append(nxt)
    return order

def dfs(graph, node, seen=None):
    if seen is None:
        seen = set()
    seen.add(node)
    order = [node]
    for nxt in graph[node]:
        if nxt not in seen:
            order += dfs(graph, nxt, seen)
    return order

BFS uses a queue, so nodes closest to the start are processed first. That makes it the tool for shortest paths when every edge costs the same. DFS uses recursion (or an explicit stack) and goes deep before backtracking. Both need a seen set, or a graph with cycles would loop forever. Both run in O(V + E) time.

Try it: Number of islands

MediumPriority

A grid of "1" (land) and "0" (water) is given as a list of lists. Count the islands. An island is land connected up, down, left or right.

11000
11000
00100
00011      ->  3 islands
Show solution and explanation
def num_islands(grid):
    if not grid:
        return 0
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])

    def sink(r, c):                             # flood-fill: turn a whole island into water
        if r < 0 or c < 0 or r >= rows or c >= cols or grid[r][c] != "1":
            return
        grid[r][c] = "0"
        sink(r + 1, c)
        sink(r - 1, c)
        sink(r, c + 1)
        sink(r, c - 1)

    count = 0
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if grid[r][c] == "1":
                count += 1                      # found a new island
                sink(r, c)
    return count

Scan every cell. When you find land, you have found a new island, so count it, and then use DFS to flood-fill (sink) the entire island to water, so it is never counted again. Time O(rows × cols), and space O(rows × cols) in the worst case for the recursion. Mention that you modified the input grid, and that you could use a separate seen set if the input must stay unchanged. Very deep recursion can hit Python's recursion limit on huge grids, and BFS with a queue avoids that.

DSA concept questions

Say each answer out loud in about 30 seconds, then open it and compare.

Recursion vs iteration?
Recursion solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller input, and is often shorter and clearer for trees and graphs. Iteration uses loops, and avoids the call-stack cost and the risk of a stack overflow. Every recursion needs a base case, or it never stops.
What is dynamic programming?
A technique for problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. Instead of recomputing the same sub-answers, you store them. Memoization does this top-down (recursion plus a cache), while tabulation does it bottom-up (filling a table).
Greedy vs dynamic programming?
Greedy takes the best-looking choice at each step and never reconsiders. It is fast but only correct for some problems. DP considers all the choices through stored sub-answers, so it is always correct when the problem has the right structure. Coin change with coins 1, 3, 4 is the standard example where greedy fails.
Adjacency list vs adjacency matrix?
A list stores only the edges that exist, giving O(V + E) space and fast iteration over neighbours, so it is best for sparse graphs. A matrix uses O(V²) space but checks whether an edge exists in O(1), which suits dense graphs.
What is amortized time complexity?
The average cost per operation over a long sequence, even if a single operation is occasionally expensive. Appending to a Python list is amortized O(1): it is normally cheap, and the occasional resize is spread out over many appends.
Best, average and worst case?
The fastest, typical and slowest running time for an input of size n. Quicksort is O(n log n) on average but O(n²) in the worst case. Interviewers usually want the worst case unless you say otherwise.
What does in-place mean?
The algorithm changes the input directly and uses only O(1) extra space, rather than building a new copy. Many array problems ask for it, and it usually means using two pointers or swaps.
Hash table vs balanced BST for storing data?
A hash table gives O(1) average lookup, but its keys are unordered. A balanced BST gives O(log n) operations, but keeps keys in sorted order, so range queries and "next larger key" are easy.
How do you approach a problem you have never seen?
Restate it, work a small example by hand, write the brute force and its complexity, look for what is repeated or wasted, and match it to a pattern (hashmap, two pointers, sliding window, stack, DP). Then code and test. Saying this process aloud is worth as much as the answer.

Day 2Module 9, about 150 minutes

SQL

SQL is asked in almost every technical round, both as theory and as "write a query on this table". You get better by writing queries against real data, so this module gives you a small bank database and ten problems.

Set up your practice database

Python ships with SQLite, so you need nothing to install. Save this schema as schema.sql. It creates four tables and fills them with data:

CREATE TABLE departments (
    id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT
);
CREATE TABLE employees (
    id            INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name          TEXT,
    salary        INTEGER,
    department_id INTEGER,
    manager_id    INTEGER
);
CREATE TABLE customers (
    id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INTEGER,
    amount      INTEGER
);

INSERT INTO departments VALUES (1, 'Engineering'), (2, 'Operations'), (3, 'Finance'), (4, 'Legal');
INSERT INTO employees VALUES
    (1, 'Asha',   90000, 1, NULL),
    (2, 'Rahul',  70000, 1, 1),
    (3, 'Meera',  95000, 1, 1),
    (4, 'Karan',  50000, 2, NULL),
    (5, 'Sana',   50000, 2, 4),
    (6, 'Vikram', 60000, 3, NULL),
    (7, 'Neha',   60000, 3, 6),
    (8, 'Arjun',  45000, 2, 4);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Amit'), (2, 'Bhavna'), (3, 'Chirag');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 1, 500), (2, 1, 300), (3, 3, 700);

Then run any query with this short script (it needs SQLite 3.25 or newer for window functions, which any current Python has):

import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
with open("schema.sql") as f:                 # the schema above, saved as schema.sql
    conn.executescript(f.read())

query = """
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 3
"""
for row in conn.execute(query):
    print(row)

Change the query text and run it again for each exercise. Here is what the tables contain:

TableColumnsNotes
employeesid, name, salary, department_id, manager_id8 rows. manager_id points at another employee, and is NULL for the top of a team
departmentsid, nameEngineering, Operations, Finance, Legal (Legal has no employees)
customersid, nameAmit, Bhavna, Chirag
ordersid, customer_id, amountAmit has two orders, Chirag one, Bhavna none

Ideas to know before you write queries

Logical order of execution. You write SELECT first, but the database evaluates a query in this order: FROM and JOIN, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT. That explains why WHERE cannot use an aggregate like COUNT(*) (groups do not exist yet), while HAVING can.

JoinReturns
INNER JOINOnly rows that match on both sides
LEFT JOINAll rows from the left table, and matches from the right (NULL where there is none)
RIGHT JOINThe mirror image of LEFT JOIN
FULL OUTER JOINAll rows from both sides, matched where possible
Self joinA table joined to itself under two aliases, such as employee and manager

NULL is not a value
